channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Overtraining may disrupt the brain's dopamine regulation, leaving levels elevated during rest
item.description: Excessive physical exercise affects more than just the muscles; it can also alter brain chemistry. A new study published in the journal Neuroscience reveals that exhaustive training without adequate rest alters the regulation of dopamine in the hippocampus, a brain region closely linked to memory and the regulation of emotions.

item.title: Could consciousness begin deep in the brain? Researchers make the case
item.description: Close your eyes and cover your ears. Much of the world around you disappears from view and hearing, yet your sense of being present, of being conscious, remains. What creates that basic feeling of being "you"?

item.title: Mechanical thrombectomy linked to lower mortality in intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism
item.description: New research presented at TCT 2026 and simultaneously published in JSCAI found that, in the primary analysis, mechanical thrombectomy was associated with lower short- and long-term mortality among patients with intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism compared with anticoagulation alone.

item.title: Children's e-bike injuries increase 33% per quarter as e-scooter injuries climb 15%
item.description: Rates of electric bike and electric scooter injuries are rising in children and teens across the country, a new Stanford Medicine–led study has found.

item.title: Understanding vertigo: Spinning, moving sensations differ from dizziness, expert explains
item.description: Vertigo is a sensation that either you or your surroundings, or both, are spinning or moving when they are not. Some people confuse vertigo with dizziness, but there is a difference, explains Neil Shepard, Ph.D., an audiologist at Mayo Clinic in Minnesota.

item.title: In parallel mouse studies, researchers fail to replicate many reported effects of psilocybin
item.description: Experimental trials of psychedelic drugs in both humans and animals have produced conflicting results, creating doubts about whether hallucinogens have a therapeutic role in treating neurologic or behavioral disorders such as depression and PTSD.

item.title: Human dengue trial reveals how immune memory can help—or backfire
item.description: Spread through the bite of Aedes mosquitoes, dengue is a viral infection that can cause anything from mild fever, flu-like symptoms and joint pain to a severe form known as dengue hemorrhagic fever. What makes dengue particularly unusual and dangerous is that a second infection with a different strain, or serotype, can sometimes lead to more severe disease rather than stronger immunity.

item.title: Depressive symptoms and aggressive behavior in children following 2024 earthquake linked to later loneliness
item.description: A research team led by associate professor Yasuo Murayama of Kanazawa University has identified longitudinal associations among loneliness, depressive symptoms and social behaviors in children affected by the 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake.

item.title: Simulated heart failure appointments uncover shared consultation patterns among doctors across four countries
item.description: Whether in Beijing, Ankara, Groningen or Würzburg, doctors treat patients with heart failure in remarkably similar ways. Not only are the medical procedures similar, but so are the questions doctors ask, their gestures and the way consultations unfold. This is the finding of an international study led by sociologists Anja Weiß and Tao Liu from the University of Duisburg-Essen (UDE). The findings, recently published in Global Networks, are also relevant to the debate on the recognition of foreign qualifications.

item.title: Simple exercises and workplace changes may help Florida landscape workers manage back pain
item.description: Hundreds of thousands of nursery and landscape workers in Florida knuckle through low back pain daily, putting them at risk for chronic discomfort, injuries and job loss. But an ongoing study on self-managed back pain in the horticulture and landscape industry finds that simple techniques could help improve their overall quality of life.

item.title: Restricting candy may increase kids' urge to overeat, research suggests
item.description: Kids and candy are a classic pairing. From trick-or-treating to Easter baskets to local parades and birthday parties, it can feel like kids are almost always bringing home another bag of treats. But while these holidays and events may be exciting for kids, they often end with parents dreading what comes next: negotiations around how much candy to consume.

item.title: Toddlers need to move, too
item.description: Physical activity among schoolchildren and teens gets plenty of attention. But what about babies who spend time strapped into car seats, toddlers who travel in strollers and preschoolers who run, climb and hop?

item.title: New treatment approach for calcified nodules shown to improve coronary stent expansion
item.description: A randomized clinical trial at The Mount Sinai Hospital found that combining two techniques for removing calcium nodules—rotational atherectomy and intravascular lithotripsy (IVL)—before coronary stent placement allowed stents to expand more fully than IVL alone in patients with calcified coronary nodules.

item.title: Beyond 'just lose weight': How gyms and clinics can welcome people of all sizes
item.description: Have you ever gone to your general practitioner to find out why you're always tired, only to be told to lose weight?

item.title: Cholesterol transport protein emerges as possible target for Parkinson's treatment
item.description: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a neurodegenerative condition that causes the progressive loss of dopamine-producing neurons in a brain region called the substantia nigra. Its characteristic symptoms include tremors, slowed movements, rigid muscles and difficulties with balance.

item.title: Q&A: The science behind the fall time change
item.description: When clocks fall back this weekend, we'll gain an hour—but does that necessarily mean better sleep? Hannah Peach, a sleep health expert at UNC Charlotte, explains how the change from daylight saving time back to standard time affects our internal body clocks, why the fall transition is easier on our bodies than the spring change and how shorter days can affect our well-being. She also explains why permanent standard time may be the healthier option, particularly for children and adolescents.

item.title: Swedish dietary surveys link higher ultraprocessed food intake to poorer nutrition
item.description: A higher proportion of ultraprocessed food in the diet is generally associated with poorer dietary quality and, among adults, a somewhat higher prevalence of overweight and obesity. This is shown by a study that also critically examines the concept of ultraprocessed foods.

item.title: Hypertension or diabetes before pregnancy linked to higher risk of fetal heart defects
item.description: Women with chronic hypertension (high blood pressure before pregnancy or diagnosed before 20 weeks of pregnancy) had a 30% higher risk of having a baby with critical congenital heart disease, the most severe form of heart defects, when compared to women with normal blood pressure before and during pregnancy, according to new independent, preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, held Nov. 6–9 in Chicago.

item.title: Cardiac arrest ICU admissions rose with outdoor heat, especially in women, older adults
item.description: As daily temperatures climbed above 90 degrees Fahrenheit (F) (32 degrees Celsius) across the U.S., so did the rate of out-of-hospital (OHCA) cardiac arrest admissions to hospitals' intensive care units (ICUs). However, the heat didn't appear to affect the overall outcomes of people admitted for cardiac arrest during heat waves compared with other times, according to new, independent, preliminary research to be presented at the American Heart Association's Resuscitation Science Symposium 2026.

item.title: Wearable devices + AI analysis may predict high blood pressure crisis up to 3 days early
item.description: Using artificial intelligence (AI) to analyze patterns in measurements from a portable cuff-based blood pressure monitor and health data from a wrist-worn device may help identify when adults with stage 2 high blood pressure (blood pressure ≥140/90 mm Hg) are at increased risk of a dangerously high blood pressure episode (>180/120 mm Hg with acute end-organ damage), known as a hypertensive crisis, up to three days before it occurs, according to new, independent, preliminary research to be presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026.

item.title: Cannabis use linked to an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, especially strokes
item.description: Cannabis use, including marijuana, appears to be linked with increased cardiovascular risk, especially for stroke, making it an important consideration for heart disease and stroke prevention and counseling, according to independent, new preliminary research to be presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026. The meeting is Nov. 6–9 in Chicago.

item.title: Survey finds gaps in use of cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome tools
item.description: In a survey of health clinics participating in a new initiative to improve care for cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome, most sites reported conducting basic screening for heart, kidney and metabolic risks. However, far fewer are using newer guideline-recommended tools such as the CKM syndrome staging framework and the American Heart Association's PREVENT (Predicting Risk of cardiovascular EVENT) equations, according to new, preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, held Nov. 6–9 in Chicago.

item.title: Retired NFL players, notably linemen, have high risk of artery plaque, independent study shows
item.description: Retired NFL players may have a high risk of undiagnosed, untreated coronary artery disease (CAD) that often occurs without symptoms, according to new, independent, preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, held Nov. 6–9 in Chicago.

item.title: Energy drinks, stimulant products linked to cardiac arrest, heart attack in young adults
item.description: Caffeinated energy drinks and stimulant supplements appeared disproportionately more often in FDA reports of serious cardiovascular events, including cardiac arrest and heart attacks, especially among adults ages 18 to 34, according to new, independent, preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, held Nov. 6–9 in Chicago.

item.title: Non-experts with AI guidance and off-site review perform quality mobile rural heart scans
item.description: Artificial intelligence (AI) helped health professionals with no ultrasound experience capture quality heart scans in rural communities for review by off-site experts, according to new, independent preliminary research to be presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026. The meeting takes place Nov. 6–9 in Chicago.

item.title: Is a consistent sleep schedule important to heart health?
item.description: Maintaining a consistent sleep schedule may be an important factor to consider for protecting the heart, according to new, independent, preliminary research to be presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026. The meeting is Nov. 6–9 in Chicago.

item.title: Medically tailored meals improve high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes and diet in adults
item.description: An eight-month program providing medically tailored meals improved diet quality and access to healthy food for adults with type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure. It also enhanced cardiometabolic health (heart, blood vessels and metabolism) by lowering blood pressure and blood sugar, according to new, independent preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, held Nov. 6–9 in Chicago.

item.title: Deaths from heart valve disease rising among U.S. adults ages 65 and older
item.description: After nearly two decades of decline, valvular heart disease death rates have increased from 2018 to 2023 and are predicted to remain elevated through 2040, according to independent, new preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, held Nov. 6–9 in Chicago.

item.title: Transportation noise linked to higher risk of heart conditions, even with healthy sleep
item.description: Adults exposed to high levels of residential transportation noise from traffic (cars and buses), as well as planes and trains, faced a higher risk of serious heart-related events and a higher likelihood of developing cardiovascular risk factors, such as high cholesterol, high blood pressure or diabetes, even among people with healthy sleep, according to new, independent, preliminary research to be presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026. The meeting will take place Nov. 6–9 in Chicago.

item.title: GLP-1 meds linked to lower diabetes, heart risks than standard diabetes prevention medication
item.description: GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists) medications, currently popular for weight loss, may help prevent type 2 diabetes and lower the risk of heart attack and stroke more than the standard diabetes prevention medication metformin among people with prediabetes, according to new, independent, preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026, held Nov. 6–9 in Chicago.
